related_work_items.paper_title: ImageNet-trained CNNs are biased towards texture; increasing shape bias improves accuracy and robustness

evidence.evidence_text: One of the most influential claims in this direction is that CNNs trained on ImageNet are inherently biased towards texture [8], in contrast to humans who predominantly rely on shape cues [11].

evidence.section: Rethinking Texture Bias: A Critical Look at Cue-Conflict Evaluation
evidence.evidence_text: The hypothesis that CNNs trained on ImageNet are biased towards texture was popularized by Geirhos et al. [8], who introduced a cue-conflict evaluation protocol.

This paper revisited the widely cited claim that CNNs trained on ImageNet are inherently biased towards texture. We identify critical conceptual and methodological limitations in the cue-conflict experiment popularized by Geirhos et al. [8] that support this hypothesis.

related_work_items.gap_relevance_note: Geirhos et al. is the central prior work the paper re-examines and challenges; the paper's main gap is framed as limitations in that cue-conflict-based texture-bias claim.

related_work_items.paper_title: The Origins and Prevalence of Texture Bias in Convolutional Neural Networks

evidence.evidence_text: Hermann et al. [13] showed that texture bias in CNNs arises primarily from training objectives and augmentations, with techniques like blurring and cropping increasing shape bias more than architectural changes.
These findings challenge the notion of fixed architectural biases and instead position feature reliance as a flexible property shaped by optimization objectives and domain-specific semantics.

related_work_items.gap_relevance_note: This work is used to shift the explanation of feature reliance from architecture to training, which directly informs the present paper's argument that texture bias is not inherent.

evidence.evidence_text: Vision transformers (ViTs) exhibit lower texture bias due to their global attention mechanism [19], [20], and vision-language models show improved alignment with human-like shape use [21].

Among transformer-based models, the ViT demonstrates a feature reliance profile similar to ResNet50-sota across all suppression conditions, challenging the notion that transformers are inherently more shape-oriented than CNNs.

related_work_items.gap_relevance_note: ViT-related prior claims serve as a comparison point that the paper qualifies by showing similar reliance profiles under its suppression-based evaluation.

related_work_items.paper_title: Are convolutional neural networks or transformers more like human vision

evidence.evidence_text: Vision transformers (ViTs) exhibit lower texture bias due to their global attention mechanism [19], [20], and vision-language models show improved alignment with human-like shape use [21].

Notably, the CLIP VIT model most closely matches human performance across all feature suppression conditions, suggesting that vision-language supervision encourages more human-aligned representations.

related_work_items.gap_relevance_note: This work is part of the transformer-versus-CNN human-vision comparison line that the paper revisits with a different evaluation paradigm.

related_work_items.paper_title: Learning visual representations for transfer learning by suppressing texture

evidence.evidence_text: Various methods have attempted to enforce shape bias or suppress texture cues for improved robustness, including anisotropic filtering [22], edge encoding [23], style disentanglement [24], [25], and shape-focused augmentations [26], [27].

related_work_items.gap_relevance_note: This cited work represents prior attempts to suppress texture during training; the present paper instead proposes an evaluation framework that measures reliance via controlled suppression at test time.

related_work_items.paper_title: Contributions of shape, texture, and color in visual recognition

evidence.evidence_text: Ge et al. [32] and Jain et al. [17] show that disentangling and combining shape, texture, and color improve robustness and interpretability.
we propose a new domain-agnostic evaluation framework that quantifies feature reliance through systematic suppression of shape, texture, and color cues

related_work_items.gap_relevance_note: This is a close bridge work because it explicitly studies shape, texture, and color together, aligning with the present paper's three-cue suppression framework.

related_work_items.paper_title: Revisiting the shape-bias of deep learning for dermoscopic skin lesion classification

evidence.evidence_text: Nonetheless, Lucieri et al. [33] caution that in domains like MI, cue entanglement is essential and biasing towards shape may be counterproductive.
Taken together, these results suggest that feature reliance in MI varies substantially across datasets, with a common trend towards greater dependence on color information.

related_work_items.gap_relevance_note: This work directly supports the paper's cross-domain argument that shape bias is not universally desirable, especially in medical imaging.

related_work_items.paper_title: Generalisation in humans and deep neural networks

evidence.evidence_text: Efforts to increase shape bias are often motivated by the broader goal of human-model alignment. Geirhos et al. [34], [35] show that even robust models exhibit error patterns that diverge from humans, revealing a persistent consistency gap.
